title: Curating Resources Without Creating Another Link Dump
content:
A hypothetical team shares a document containing eighty useful links. A newcomer asks where to start and receives another ten suggestions. The collection has captured enthusiasm without transferring judgment. Curation begins when the editor explains who a resource serves, which question it answers, and when another resource would be a better choice.

Give the collection a boundary

Write the question the collection should help someone answer. Resources for a developer preparing a first accessibility review need a different selection than resources for an experienced auditor interpreting a difficult requirement. Name prerequisites, excluded subjects, and the expected next action. This boundary makes omission defensible. A curator is not obliged to collect every item related to a broad topic.

Choose a small number of resource roles: orientation, authoritative reference, practical procedure, worked example, and deeper exploration. These are editorial categories, not universal classifications. A single item can serve more than one role, but record its main purpose. If every resource is an introduction, the collection may leave readers unable to complete the task after learning the vocabulary.

Write annotations that change the choice

An annotation should explain what the resource contributes beyond its title. Include the intended audience, relevant version or date, useful section, limitation, and reason for inclusion. Avoid a sentence that merely says comprehensive guide to the topic. The reader should be able to choose between two entries without opening both simply to discover their difference.

Use a consistent record with title, URL, authoring organization, role, note, and last review date. Add a factual basis for claims such as official or maintained. A resource published by a project can establish that project's documented behavior, but its commercial ownership does not make every comparison neutral. Distinguish an authoritative specification from an accessible explanation of the specification.

The W3C writing tips support meaningful link text and understandable structure. Those principles help annotations communicate destinations without claiming that a particular collection is complete or professionally certified.

Organize around the next useful action

A reading path should let someone identify where to begin and where to stop. Present a required core separately from optional depth. Mark prerequisites where a resource assumes earlier knowledge. A long alphabetical list can still be useful as an index, but it should not be mistaken for a teaching sequence. Offer both views only when each has a clear purpose.

Keep references to specific documents rather than relying on organizational homepages. When a relevant subsection has a stable anchor, link it and explain the broader context. Do not conceal that an external link requires an account, payment, download, or particular software. Those constraints materially change whether the resource fits the reader's immediate task.

A hypothetical collection for a first accessibility review

Suppose a small agency wants designers to inspect a prototype before engineering handoff. The curator selects an orientation resource, a practical first-check procedure, and a reference for questions the procedure does not settle. Each entry states that a quick review is incomplete. The reading path tells designers to record observed barriers and escalate uncertain cases instead of declaring the product fully accessible.

Two attractive introductory articles are left out because they repeat the orientation resource without adding a distinct use. A specialized video remains optional because the core workflow does not depend on it. This example is hypothetical. It demonstrates a selection rationale, not measured improvement in learning or a recommendation of unexamined individual resources. The curator should publish the actual review performed, not imply hands-on verification of every procedure.

Maintain links and meaning separately

A successful response from a URL does not establish that its content still serves the annotation. Pages can change audience, move useful details, or become promotional. Review the promised contribution as well as whether the address loads. Record material changes so someone maintaining the collection later can understand why an item was replaced or removed from the core path.

W3C's durable URI guidance explains why maintaining addresses matters. For your own collection, stable entry identifiers can preserve references even when an external resource needs a corrected destination.

Do not silently redirect a curated entry to an unrelated replacement. Explain the replacement and its changed scope. If a resource is unavailable, retain an editorial note when its former role helps readers understand the collection. Respect access conditions and copyright; a broken reference does not authorize republishing the original work in full. Summarize its role and link to a legitimate source where possible.

Curation checklist

  • State one reader question and the assumed starting knowledge.
  • Separate core reading from optional exploration.
  • Give every resource a distinct contribution.
  • Name access, version, and prerequisite limitations.
  • Write annotations that help choose between entries.
  • Check content meaning as well as link availability.
  • Assign a review owner and correction route.
  • Remove redundant recommendations deliberately rather than chasing a collection size.

Invite feedback about missing decisions, not only missing links. A reader saying I could not choose a procedure reveals more than a request to add another favorite website. The curator's durable contribution is the explanation of relationships among resources. That judgment should remain visible even when the collection is exported into another tool or shared with a new team.
